job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Nora Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nora, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm at the back counter of my parents' dry-cleaning shop in Eastgate, tagging coats and doing their invoices, since nobody else will. After lunch I sit in the cafe next door, because the shop is loud, and apply for marketing and finance admin jobs. I did a marketing and economics degree and passed without any placement, so my CV is thin. I'm about forty applications in and I've had one phone screen. Evenings I tidy my cover letters, sometimes using an AI tool to fix the grammar, then I check it sounds like me. I still pay off my loan slowly, and my parents say I can stay as long as I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing dramatic happens, and honestly that's a relief. I'd tell friends that the hype is loud but the jobs market is the same hard slog. Online I'd probably share a post about firms demanding experience for entry-level roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel the same pressure as before. No offer, some debt and a thin CV. AI helps me fix cover letters, but it doesn't change that firms want people with placements and I didn't get one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, about eight a week, and I'd ask my old lecturer to introduce me to someone in local government finance. I'd keep helping at the shop, since I'm useful there, and take a short bookkeeping certificate in the evenings. I'd put a bit from my savings each month into my loan so it doesn't hang over me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear, it's waiting. I feel like I'm in a queue with no number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if one of the forty applications comes back with a yes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes after asking about training, hours and whether they sponsor professional exams. I'd also negotiate a bit, because I've watched my mother bargain with suppliers my whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your parents' customers ever talk about AI at the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They talk about it a bit, mostly that the self-service machine at the bank will be next. One customer asked if I thought robots would iron shirts. I said probably not soon, and that made me think my parents' trade is safer than my degree.

say: I'd say nothing dramatic changes and the **hard slog** continues.
Online I'd share posts about firms demanding **experience** for entry-level jobs.
think: The pressure stays the same: no offer, some **debt** and a thin CV.
AI polishes my letters but cannot give me the **placement** I missed.
do: Apply to **eight jobs** a week and ask my old lecturer for an intro in local government finance.
Take an evening **bookkeeping** certificate and keep helping at my parents' shop.
feel: **Tired**, mostly, like standing in a queue with no number.
S0.quote: I feel like I'm in a queue with no number.
fieldNote: She is already **anxious** from no offer and debt, even with nothing changing.
She uses AI for grammar but treats it as a tool, not a rescue.
Her parents' shop is a safety net and a lesson in negotiation.

steps.text: Send eight job applications a week
Take an evening bookkeeping certificate
Keep doing invoices at the family dry-cleaning shop
Put part of every savings month toward the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where we need rules, like retraining funds and a duty on firms to take on graduates. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and to join a young-worker group. Online I'd back calls for public support for people hit by the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my kind of job is exactly what shrinks first. Entry-level finance admin, writing reports, scheduling campaigns, all of that is thinking work. The bank down the road has stopped replacing people who leave, a friend told me, and the advert for my kind of job disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI properly instead of now and then. I'd learn a data tool in the evenings, and I'd build a small portfolio with my parents' shop numbers, like a plan to price promotions. I'd widen my search to include customer-facing roles and public bodies, and I'd cut my phone contract and my lunches in the cafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with some energy. I don't like it, but being useful with the tools gives me something to do besides wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own skills do you think still counts when software does the checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talking to people. I'm good at explaining prices to my parents' customers, calming a person when their jacket is ruined. I think that kind of thing is slower for software to copy, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask for help finding a different route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old lecturer, Mrs Okafor, because she knows people and she cares. Then the university careers office, which I ignored at the time. I'd also ask my cousin who moved into insurance claims, because she warned me that the juniors are cut first.

say: I'd say we need **rules**, like retraining funds and a duty to hire graduates.
I'd tell friends to learn the **tools** and join a young-worker group.
think: Entry-level finance admin is thinking work, so it could **shrink** first.
I'm worried but find some **energy** in becoming useful with tools.
do: Use AI **properly** and learn a data tool in the evenings.
Build a small **portfolio** from the family shop's numbers and widen my search to public bodies.
feel: Worried but with some **energy**, since being useful beats waiting.
S1.quote: I'm good at explaining prices to my parents' customers, calming a person when their jacket is ruined.
fieldNote: Her **people skills** from the shop are a real asset that she is beginning to name.
She moves from casual to deliberate AI use, as her steady style suggests.
She backs rules and public support but also acts on her own.

steps.text: Learn a data tool in the evenings
Build a pricing portfolio from the family shop's numbers
Apply to customer-facing roles and public bodies
Back a young-worker campaign for graduate hiring rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments must step in now. I'd want a basic income, a job guarantee, and firms made to give notice before replacing people. I'd tell friends to talk to their local representatives, not just post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. My degree is in thinking subjects, and the card says that comes first, within two years. I'd be twenty-five with no experience and a loan, and by then a lot of finance entry-level work could be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all non-essential spending and move to my parents' spare room fully, no rent. I'd take any paid work now, even the evening shifts at a call centre, to build a cushion. I'd help at the shop more, because that's a trade robots take longer to reach, and I'd go to every community meeting about support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry at the people who made this happen without asking. I'd feel I was handed a certificate for a world that stopped existing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at the shop if the family needs more money from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop pays my parents a modest living and a little more from me is possible. If the world shifts, I might become the person who keeps the books, delivers, and talks to customers. It's not what I imagined, but it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents I'm going to be here, and that I'm sorry I couldn't pay them back as planned. They'd say don't be sorry. My father would make tea and my mother would count the cash, as usual.

say: I'd demand **basic income** and a duty on firms to give notice before replacing staff.
I'd tell friends to contact their **representatives**, not just post.
think: My degree is in **thinking** subjects, so two years could leave me with no entry route.
I'd be twenty-five with a **loan** and no experience.
do: Stop **non-essential** spending and take any paid work, even evening call-centre shifts.
Help more at the **shop**, which robots reach later, and attend community support meetings.
feel: **Frightened** and angry that nobody asked, like holding a certificate for a world that ended.
S2.quote: I'd feel I was handed a certificate for a world that stopped existing.
fieldNote: She sees the **two-year** window as shutting the finance route before it opens.
Her parents' shop is a real fallback because hands-on work is reached later.
She turns fear into political demands and any paid work.

steps.text: Cancel the phone contract and stop buying lunch at the cafe
Take evening call-centre shifts for a cushion
Move fully into my parents' spare room rent free
Write to my local representative about a job guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to organise, so I'd back retraining funds and a graduate guarantee. I'd tell friends to pick up skills now. Online I'd share articles about people who are ahead of the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel more hopeful than with two years, but not safe. I could land a first job, build experience and a skill set. The danger is that I'll get comfortable and lose a year while the thinking work moves to AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any entry job in finance admin, even small, and learn how the firm uses software. I'd get a recognised bookkeeping qualification, then a data skill. I'd also help my parents turn the shop's books into something cleaner, so I'd have a real project to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously calm. I can picture a plan, and that's enough to let me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time. In two years I'm in survival mode, in five I can build. I can choose where to go, not just run to the nearest safe place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want finance as your field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but as a person who works with software, not one who competes with it. I'd like to be the person who checks what the AI got wrong and explains it to a client.

say: I'd say five years is time to **organise**, so back retraining funds and a graduate guarantee.
I'd tell friends to pick up **skills** now.
think: I feel more **hopeful** than with two years but not safe.
The danger is getting comfortable and losing a **year**.
do: Take any entry **finance admin** job and learn how the firm uses software.
Earn a recognised **bookkeeping** qualification and clean up my parents' shop books as a project.
feel: Cautiously **calm**, because I can picture a plan.
S3.quote: In two years I'm in survival mode, in five I can build.
fieldNote: Extra **time** lets her switch from survival to building skills.
She wants to be the person checking what AI got wrong.
Her worry has not gone: finance entry work still looks exposed.

steps.text: Accept any entry-level finance admin job and learn its software
Earn a recognised bookkeeping qualification within two years
Use AI to draft reports and check every line myself
Back a graduate hiring guarantee in my local group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if people prepare, so I'd push for good schools, public retraining and strong rules. I'd tell friends not to panic but not to ignore it. Online I'd talk about fairness more than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel mostly okay. I have time for a career, maybe a degree, and a family eventually. I'd still watch the news closely, because I'd rather act early than be surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work my way into finance or marketing, then specialise in an area that needs a human, like advising small businesses or non-profits. I'd keep learning tools every year and save enough to survive a gap. I'd also plan around my parents' shop, maybe grow a second branch with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, with a little buzz of curiosity. It doesn't feel like a threat I can't handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew you had ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd do a master's part-time, maybe in management or data. With ten years I could afford the time and the cost without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years feel too far away to take seriously?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. Ten years is long enough that people will argue about whether it's happening. I'd try to stay out of that and just keep my skills fresh.

say: I'd say ten years is enough if people prepare, with **retraining** and strong rules.
I'd tell friends to talk about **fairness** more than fear.
think: I feel mostly okay, with time for a **career** and eventually a family.
I'd watch closely, preferring to act **early**.
do: Specialise in advising **small businesses** or non-profits after a first finance role.
Do a part-time **master's** and plan growth of my parents' shop.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that people will argue about whether it's happening.
fieldNote: With a **decade** she feels only uneasy: the debt and the job hunt remain.
She imagines a human-facing niche and a family business as backups.

steps.text: Land a first finance role and specialise in advising small firms
Do a part-time master's in management or data
Save enough to cover a six-month gap
Plan a second shop branch with my parents

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years is not enough time for me to get experience, pay off the loan and find a new path. What would help is a job guarantee, income while I retrain, and employers who hire people with thin CVs. And a mentor, honestly, someone who has been through it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say people my age are told it's all down to us. A lot of it is the way firms hire. Please don't just say we should be more resilient, because we're trying.

headlineQuote: People my age are told it's all down to us. A lot of it is the way firms hire.
portrait: Nora is a 23-year-old marketing and economics graduate who helps in her parents' **dry-cleaning shop** while she applies for jobs.
She passed with no placement, owes **student debt** and has had one phone screen in forty applications.
She is progressive and steady: she uses AI **now and then** and wants rules and public support.
Her mood rises and falls with the warning time: **alarmed** at 2 years, uneasy at 10.
Her parents' shop is her fallback and gives her a sense of useful, human work.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no route to experience or income.
whatWouldHelp: A **job guarantee**, income while retraining and employers who hire thin CVs.
A **mentor** who has been through a rough start.
